regenerable_on: a guest running libvirtd with the python bindings installed and at least one domain defined — the payload is `_domains_raw()`, which opens the read-only socket through libvirt-python (the [vms] extra), so a guest carrying the daemon but not the bindings produces no payload at all
note:
One defined, shut-off domain on a lab guest's libvirt: the smallest capture that is still a real domain rather than a fixture. Scrubbed with the keyed manifest scrubber against harness/scrub/vms.json — the domain UUID and the NIC MAC are substituted in BOTH places they appear, the member and the XML, because the same identifier in two spellings is the join a reader would otherwise have to take on trust, and the operator-chosen domain name went through --hostnames like any other word somebody typed.

What it exists to teach is the shape of a NOT-running guest, which is where the address facts are decided. A shut-off domain has no address BECAUSE IT IS OFF — that is inapplicability, not emptiness and not unobservability — so IPAddresses is omitted from the row entirely rather than published as [] or as null with a reason beside it. All three spellings look alike in a table and mean different things: [] claims the guest has no address, null claims the value exists and could not be read, and omission claims the question does not arise. An appliance guest once read [] while answering on its own address, which is why the distinction has a rule (SPEC section 2 rule 7) and why this variant anchors the absence rather than a value.

The row is the SUMMARY subset, not the domain's whole fact set: the collection publishes State, MemoryMiB, VCPUs, Autostart, Persistent and HostTaps and drops the XML-derived detail the opened object carries. HostTaps rides on the row deliberately — it is the only authoritative answer to which domain owns a given vnet device, and a consumer looking at network/links wants every tap from one request. Here it is empty, and empty is the truth: this NIC sits on libvirt's `default` network with no <target dev=…/> element, so the host side of it has no name this collector may claim.

Stated bounds, because a specimen shows one machine on one day. The guest is not running, so no address is exercised by replay at all — the differential guard's `libvirt-running-guest` operator owns that shape, and IPAddresses is reached by nothing else. memory_mib and max_memory_mib are both 256 here, so a port that read the wrong member into MemoryMiB passes this pair; a guest ballooned below its maximum is what would tell them apart. And there is one domain, on no bridge, with no passed-through device — so multi-domain ordering, the bridge and tap facts with something in them, and the PCI/USB hostdev paths are all unvisited by this capture.
anchors_note:
Read off payloads/domains.json by hand at staging, before any stream was generated, which is what makes them an authority the reference-generated half is not. Every value is the scrubbed spelling, which is what the committed payload carries: the object name is the domain's own name, `host-7a173d` after the scrub, and nothing here is transcribed from the reference's output.

State, MemoryMiB, VCPUs, Autostart and Persistent come straight off the domain's own members — `dom.info()` and the two flag calls — and they are typed as well as valued: Autostart false and Persistent true are BOOLEANS, VCPUs and MemoryMiB are INTEGERS, and the corpus judge compares under typed equality, so a port that shipped "false" or 256.0 fails here and would fail a typed consumer for the same reason.

HostTaps [] is asserted rather than left unstated because empty is a claim: the NIC element carries <source network='default'/> and no <target dev=…/>, so there is no host-side tap to name. A port that invented one from the MAC — the fe:54:/52:54: resemblance is a QEMU convention and not a record — or that read the `network` attribute as a bridge, fails here.

The two absences are the point of the variant. IPAddresses is absent because the guest is off, and IPAddressesUnobservable is absent because there is nothing to explain: the pair means "running, and this agent cannot see the address", and asserting both halves absent is what refuses a port that publishes the reason without the value, or [] for a domain that was never asked.

commit_objects 1 is the count of entries in the payload list. It is anchored because absent is not the only way to lose a collection: a port that emitted the domain twice, or that emitted a row per NIC rather than per domain, gets a different number and every fact anchor above would still pass.

Deliberately not anchored: the domain UUID and the NIC MAC. Both are in the payload and neither reaches the row, so an anchor on them would assert something about the opened object this collection does not publish — and the values are substitutions, which makes them an authority about the scrubber rather than about the machine.
